examples.label: a*b*  (right-linear)
examples.purpose: Regular languages have right-linear grammars: each step extends the word on the right.
text: S -> a S | b B | eps

examples.label: (ab)+  (left-linear)
examples.purpose: A left-linear grammar: the word grows on the left of the nonterminal.
text: // Rules: A -> B w  (nonterminal on the left of the terminal)
// Compare with the right-linear version: S -> a B, B -> b S | b
S -> S a b | a b

examples.label: Even number of a's  (left-linear)
examples.purpose: A counting language as a grammar: the nonterminals remember the parity.
text: // Left-linear grammar for strings over {a,b} with an even number of a's
// S = even count so far (accepting);  A = odd count so far
// Rules: A -> B w  (nonterminal then terminal)
S -> A a | S b | eps

examples.label: Strings ending in ab  (right-linear)
examples.purpose: The classic suffix language: nonterminals track progress toward the final ab.
text: S -> a S | b S | a A

examples.label: Balanced a…b  (aⁿbⁿ)
examples.purpose: The standard non-regular context-free language: matching pairs built from the outside in.

examples.label: Palindromes over {a, b}
examples.purpose: Rules that mirror: each step adds a matching symbol on both sides.
text: S -> a S a | b S b | a | b | eps

examples.label: Left-recursive expressions
examples.purpose: Operator precedence built into the grammar's structure.

examples.label: Ambiguous arithmetic
examples.purpose: One string, two derivation trees: try different orders to find them.
text: // to see two distinct derivations for the same string
E -> E + E | E * E | ( E ) | id

examples.label: Dangling else
examples.purpose: The classic ambiguity of nested conditionals.
text: S -> if S then S else S | if S then S | a

examples.label: LL(1) arithmetic
examples.purpose: The same expressions as the left-recursive grammar, rewritten for top-down parsing.

examples.label: Equal numbers of a and b
examples.purpose: Context-free but not regular: any order of a and b, with balanced counts.
text: A -> a | a S | b A A
B -> b | b S | a B B

examples.label: Matched parentheses
examples.purpose: Nested balanced parentheses, the standard Dyck language.

examples.label: aⁿbⁿcⁿ  (n ≥ 1)
examples.purpose: The standard context-sensitive language: not context-free.
text: // LHS sequences use uppercase convention for non-terminals
// Step 1: build a string of n copies of [BC] using S
// Step 2: sort BC pairs left-to-right using CB -> BC
// Step 3: replace leading aB with ab, then cascade b/c
S -> a B c | a S B c

examples.label: aⁿbⁿcⁿdⁿ  (n ≥ 1)
examples.purpose: Four-way counting: the same technique with one more symbol.
text: // Uses marker nonterminals B, C, D that bubble right into place
S -> a B c D | a S B c D

examples.label: Equal a's and b's  (aⁿbⁿ, n ≥ 1)
examples.purpose: A context-free language written with context-sensitive rules for comparison.
text: // (also context-free, shown here with CSG rules for comparison)
S -> a S b | a b

examples.label: Copy language  (ww)
examples.purpose: Unrestricted rules copy a word; ww is not context-free.
text: // Uses marker X to split and align two copies
X -> X a A | X b B | eps
